key_facts: **Androgenetic alopecia** (male- and female-pattern hair loss) is the commonest cause of hair loss: genetic sensitivity of follicles to androgens.
Men: temporal recession and vertex thinning (Hamilton–Norwood); women: diffuse crown thinning with a **preserved frontal hairline** and widened parting (Ludwig).
Topical **minoxidil** 2% or 5% for both sexes (continuous, about 6 months to judge); **finasteride 1 mg** in men.
In women with signs of hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism, irregular periods) check for PCOS or another cause.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Androgenetic alopecia (AGA)** is genetically predisposed, androgen-mediated, progressive **follicular miniaturisation**.

head: Male pattern (MPHL)
Female pattern (FPHL)
rows: Mid-frontal and crown thinning with a **widened parting** (‘Christmas tree’); **frontal hairline usually preserved** (Ludwig/Sinclair)
Usually **normal**. Check for PCOS if there are acne, hirsutism or irregular periods

sub: About half of men by 50 and up to 40% of women by 70.
Strong family history; onset after puberty.

ul: **DHT** (from testosterone via 5α-reductase) shortens anagen and miniaturises follicles in a genetically susceptible scalp.
Polygenic inheritance from **both** sides of the family.
Women with true hyperandrogenism may show a male-type pattern with acne, hirsutism and irregular periods (consider PCOS).
Polygenic inheritance (androgen receptor gene on the X chromosome and others).
**Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** formed by 5α-reductase in the scalp.
**"Hats or frequent washing cause baldness"**: they do not.
**"Minoxidil can be stopped once hair returns"**: stopping loses the gains within months.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: DHT gradually **shrinks** genetically susceptible scalp follicles.

mech.t: 5α-reductase type II converts testosterone to **DHT** in the follicle; finasteride blocks this step.
DHT shortens each growth phase, so hairs grow for less time and are shorter.
Each cycle produces a thinner, shorter, less pigmented hair until terminal hairs become vellus-like.
More follicles in telogen and fewer terminal hairs give see-through scalp in a patterned distribution.

histo: Rarely needed: reduced terminal-to-vellus ratio, increased telogen hairs, no scarring. Dermoscopy shows variable hair diameter (anisotrichosis).

ul: Gradual, **non-scarring** thinning with miniaturised hairs and **variable hair diameter**.
The pull test is usually **negative** (positive in telogen effluvium).
Psychological distress is common in both sexes.

sub: Usually normal androgen levels; test only if there are features of hyperandrogenism.
Spironolactone is an off-label specialist option; contraception needed.

ul: Clinical ± dermoscopy (miniaturisation, hair diameter diversity).
**Bloods** if there is sudden shedding, signs of scarring, or features of hyperandrogenism or systemic disease in women: **ferritin, TFTs**, and hormones as indicated.
Biopsy is rarely needed.

ddx.name: Scarring alopecias
ddx.f: Loss of follicle openings, redness, scale, pain. **Refer**

sections.title: Management
blocks: Check doses in the current BNF and SmPC. Off-label agents follow local dermatology advice.

ul: **Topical minoxidil** 2% or 5% for **both sexes**. It must be used continuously. An **initial shed** is possible in the first weeks. Facial hair can appear if it runs onto the face. Allow about 6 months to judge the effect.

**Oral finasteride 1 mg** (men), a type II 5α-reductase inhibitor. Counsel on **sexual and mood side effects** (MHRA warning on psychiatric effects and suicidal thoughts). It is **teratogenic to a male fetus**: contraindicated in pregnancy, and women who are or may become pregnant must not handle crushed or broken tablets. Not licensed for women of childbearing potential.

refer.t: Signs of **scarring alopecia** (lost follicle openings, inflammation, pain or itch): refer.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Signs of **scarring alopecia** (lost follicle openings, inflammation, pain or itch): refer.
Rapid or patchy loss, or a positive pull test: look for another diagnosis.
Women with acne, hirsutism and irregular periods: assess for **PCOS** or hyperandrogenism.
Mood change or sexual dysfunction on finasteride: review and stop if needed (MHRA).
Psychological distress; sunburn and actinic damage on the bald scalp.
Slowly progressive; treatment stabilises or partly reverses loss while it continues.

pearls: **Early treatment preserves more hair** than late rescue.
Stopping treatment means **gains reverse** over months, so explain this before starting.
Women: exclude scarring alopecia and reversible causes (iron, thyroid) before long-term cosmetic treatment.
Finasteride counselling must cover psychiatric and sexual side effects and pregnancy safety for partners.
PRP: avoid overselling it. Document informed expectations. Platelet disorders and anticoagulation need specialist judgement.

quiz.q: When should you think of Androgenetic alopecia (male & female)?
quiz.a: Gradual, non-scarring thinning: frontotemporal recession and vertex in men; widening central parting or crown in women.
DHT (via 5α-reductase) miniaturises genetically susceptible follicles and shortens anagen.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Topical minoxidil (both sexes) and oral finasteride 1 mg (men), started early and continued. Gains reverse on stopping.
Scarring alopecia (lost follicle openings, inflammation), hyperandrogenism in women, and telogen effluvium triggers (iron, thyroid).

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Signs of **scarring alopecia** (lost follicle openings, inflammation, pain or itch): refer.
